notes: Homelessness review appeal; rescission of s193 duty and s175 availability analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Homelessness appeal: rescinding a section 193 housing duty
key_facts: Andrea Porteous applied to West Dorset District Council as homeless with priority need and was initially accepted as owed a section 193 duty.
It later emerged she remained tenant of a Chiswick flat available to her through Hounslow Borough Council.
The council rescinded its March 2003 decision and, on review, found she was not homeless because she could return to the Chiswick property.
The County Court rejected her appeal on both grounds; she appealed to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from a County Court decision on a section 204 homelessness appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the local authority was entitled to revisit its earlier section 193 decision after discovering a fundamental mistake of fact, and the review decision that accommodation remained available was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A local housing authority may revisit and rescind an earlier decision accepting a section 193 duty where that decision rested on a fundamental mistake of fact, even absent fraud; on review the relevant date is that of the review decision, and a person is not homeless under section 175 if accommodation remains reasonably available to her.
legal_issues: Whether a local authority may rescind an earlier section 193 decision after discovering the applicant still had accommodation
Whether the applicant owed a duty of disclosure to the housing authority
Whether the applicant was homeless as at the date of the section 202 review
Whether the Chiswick property remained available to her at the review date

notes: Customs PACE Code C caution appeal; breach found but s78 exclusion refused and convictions safe.

enrichment.short_title: Drug importation appeal: PACE caution at customs questioning
key_facts: Dianne and Samantha Senior were convicted by a 10:2 majority of knowingly concerned in fraudulent evasion of prohibition on importing cocaine.
Customs officers had field-tested cocaine in suitcases before questioning the appellants in the Green Channel without cautioning them.
Dianne claimed duress; Samantha claimed no knowledge of the drugs; both received long custodial sentences.
Their airport answers were used at trial to undermine their credibility.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge, with an extension of time for one appellant.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; although there was a significant and substantial breach of PACE Code C, exclusion under section 78 was not required and the convictions were safe.
enrichment.ratio: Where customs officers already have grounds to suspect both travellers of involvement in drug importation before routine Green Channel questioning, a caution should be administered before further questions likely to be used in evidence; nevertheless, exclusion may be refused under section 78 where the questions were of a type travellers must expect, the answers were not disputed, and the convictions did not depend on the impugned answers.
legal_issues: Whether customs officers breached PACE Code C paragraph 10.1 by failing to caution before questioning
When grounds for suspicion arise in airport drug importation cases
Whether the breach was significant and substantial
Whether fairness required exclusion of the Green Channel answers under section 78
linked_authorities: Okafor [1994] 3 All ER 741
R v Nelson and Rose [1998] 2 Crim App R 399
R v Walsh 91 Cr App R 161
R v Cox (1993) 96 Cr App R 464

notes: Leasehold s45 counter-notice validity; Mannai approach and Portman Estate misnaming resolved on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Leasehold counter-notice valid despite wrong landlord name

statutes_considered.title: Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993

key_facts: Tenants at 8 Alexton Yard served a section 42 notice of claim on the Portman Family Settled Estates trustees.
The landlord's solicitors served a section 45 counter-notice naming the wrong Portman trust as landlord.
The county court struck out the landlord's section 46 proceedings on the basis the counter-notice was invalid.
Both properties were part of the Portman Estate in Central London, managed by Farrer & Co.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court strike-out of the landlord's section 46 application.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the section 45 counter-notice was valid despite misidentifying the landlord, because a reasonable recipient would have known it was authorised by the actual landlord.
enrichment.ratio: A section 45 counter-notice is not invalid merely because it misnames the landlord if a reasonable tenant recipient could be in no doubt that it was given by or on behalf of the actual landlord; the Mannai objective approach applies, and a tenant may rely on the landlord's identification unless unequivocally corrected.
legal_issues: Whether a section 45 counter-notice must correctly identify the landlord
Application of Mannai to statutory leasehold notices
Whether the tenant could reasonably treat the counter-notice as authorised by the true landlord
Effect of prior collective enfranchisement proceedings on notice validity

notes: Estate dispute on deed of trust and joint bank account; undue influence claim failed on evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Estate dispute over right-to-buy deed of trust and joint account
key_facts: Florence Bennett bought her Sutton council flat at a discount with half the price paid by her niece Valerie Gibson-West.
Miss Bennett and Mrs Gibson-West executed a deed of trust giving Mrs Gibson-West the equitable interest and proceeds of sale.
Miss Bennett later put an Abbey National current account into joint names with Mrs Gibson-West.
Miss Bennett died in 1998; her nephew Anthony Papouis challenged the deed as procured by undue influence and claimed the account formed part of the estate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial on beneficial ownership of flat and bank account following probate dispute between residuary beneficiaries.
enrichment.outcome: Undue influence claim dismissed; Mrs Gibson-West was beneficially entitled to the flat under the deed of trust, but the bank account balance at death formed part of Miss Bennett's estate subject to account and inquiry.
enrichment.ratio: Undue influence is a question of fact requiring proof of trust and confidence plus a transaction calling for explanation, or direct evidence of abuse; here the donor received independent legal advice, understood she would retain no interest in the property, and the nephew failed to establish the evidential presumption or actual undue influence.
legal_issues: Whether the deed of trust was procured by Mrs Gibson-West's undue influence
Whether Miss Bennett reposed trust and confidence in her niece in financial matters
Whether Mr Leach adequately explained the deed's effect
Whether the joint bank account passed to the surviving joint holder by survivorship
linked_authorities: Royal Bank of Scotland plc v Etridge (No. 2) [2002] 2 AC 773

confidence.notes: Findings on undue influence and the joint account are detailed and supported by contemporaneous documents.

notes: Insurance binder document access dispute; interim order granted pending arbitration on agency records.

enrichment.short_title: Hiscox access to binding authority records pending arbitration
key_facts: Hiscox appointed Dickson Manchester as underwriting agents under a binding authority agreement for professional indemnity business.
After HCC acquired DM, DM sought to move the book to an HCC group company and Hiscox gave 30 days' notice of cancellation.
Hiscox sought urgent access to policy records and producing broker details to offer renewals worth about £6.5m annually.
DM resisted access, relying on confidentiality and a 1999 undertaking not to compete for the business.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim application for inspection and copying of agency records during pending arbitration under the binding authority agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Limited interim order made granting Hiscox access to records for risks due for renewal up to the date of the arbitrator's award; jurisdiction under section 44 upheld as urgent.
enrichment.ratio: Records relating to risks written under a binding authority belong to the principal insurer, who is entitled to inspect and copy them under ordinary agency principles and clause 15; a former agent cannot withhold producing broker information to prevent the principal from renewing its own business, and section 44 permits urgent court intervention where the tribunal cannot act effectively.
legal_issues: Whether Hiscox was entitled to inspect records including producing broker identities
Whether clause 15 was limited to audit rather than post-termination renewal
Whether the court had jurisdiction to grant an interim order under section 44
Whether an October 1999 undertaking barred Hiscox from contacting brokers after termination

notes: GMC bias challenge partly succeeded; committee correctly continued but should have granted short adjournment.

enrichment.short_title: GMC fitness to practise: newspaper publicity and fair hearing
key_facts: Dr Mahfouz faced GMC Professional Conduct Committee charges relating to cosmetic laser treatment of several patients.
After the first hearing day, newspapers published prejudicial material about a prior 1987 erasure not in evidence before the committee.
Four committee members had seen the articles; Dr Mahfouz applied for the committee to discharge itself.
The committee refused and later refused a short adjournment to seek a High Court stay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review refusing to stay GMC proceedings after refusal to discharge the committee.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on bias but allowed on adjournment; the committee was entitled to continue, but should have granted a limited adjournment to allow a High Court application.
enrichment.ratio: Prejudicial publicity about prior disciplinary history does not necessarily require discharge of an experienced GMC committee applying Porter v Magill; the court makes its own judgment on fairness rather than reviewing on Wednesbury grounds, but fairness required granting a short adjournment so the practitioner could seek a stay before the hearing continued in his absence.
legal_issues: Whether committee members' exposure to prejudicial newspaper reports gave rise to apparent bias
Whether unconscious bias had to be expressly considered
Whether the committee should have adjourned to allow a High Court stay application
The role of the legal assessor in advising on natural justice issues

notes: Kehoe child support Article 6 appeal allowed; parent with care has no enforceable civil right to assessed maintenance.

enrichment.short_title: Child support enforcement and Article 6 right of access to court
key_facts: Mrs Kehoe sought a declaration that the Child Support Act 1991 was incompatible with Article 6 because she could not personally enforce maintenance arrears.
The Child Support Agency assessed and enforced maintenance, with the Secretary of State having discretion over enforcement.
Wall J held Article 6 was engaged but the scheme was compliant; both parties appealed.
Large numbers of CSA cases involved substantial outstanding maintenance, much considered uncollectable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a High Court Human Rights Act declaration application concerning child maintenance enforcement.
enrichment.outcome: Secretary of State's appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; Article 6 was not engaged because the parent with care had no arguable domestic civil right to a particular maintenance payment enforceable against the absent parent.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Child Support Act 1991 the parent with care does not have a domestic civil right to a particular maintenance sum enforceable against the absent parent; maintenance assessment and enforcement are statutory functions conferred on the Secretary of State, so Article 6 does not confer a right of access to court to pursue such payments personally.
legal_issues: Whether a parent with care has a civil right to child maintenance enforceable in court
Whether Article 6 ECHR is engaged by inability to enforce CSA arrears personally
Whether the child support scheme is Article 6 compliant
Whether judicial review provides sufficient access to court
linked_authorities: Re C (A Minor) (Contribution Notice) [1994] 1 FLR 111
Phillips v Peace [1996] 2 FCR 237

confidence.notes: Article 6 analysis and appeal outcome are clear, though the judgment contains extensive historical material on maintenance law.

notes: North Sea helicopter crash stay refused; declaratory proceedings in England appropriate for crew dependants.

enrichment.short_title: Helicopter crash litigation: stay refused for US forum shopping

statutes_considered.title: Carriage by Air (Application of Provisions) Order 1967

key_facts: A Bristow Helicopters aircraft crashed in July 2002 en route between North Sea installations, killing all on board.
Bristows blamed Sikorsky and CTI over repair and certification of a rotor blade previously damaged by lightning.
Bristows sought declaratory relief limiting liability and joined deceased crew and dependants as defendants.
Crew dependants sought a stay to pursue higher damages claims against Sikorsky in Connecticut.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to stay English proceedings and set aside Part 20 and declaratory claims against deceased crew and dependants.
enrichment.outcome: Applications dismissed; England was the clearly appropriate forum and dependants failed to show a distinctly more suitable alternative forum or discharge the Spiliada burden.
enrichment.ratio: Negative declaratory relief may properly be used to compel temporising claimants to litigate in the natural forum where the accident occurred and English law applies; defendants seeking a forum non conveniens stay bear the full Spiliada burden even when only declaratory relief is sought, and choice of forum based on higher US damages is not a relevant factor.
legal_issues: Whether declaratory proceedings against crew dependants should be stayed
Whether England or Connecticut was the appropriate forum
Whether applicable law was English or Connecticut law
Whether negative declarations were a legitimate procedural tactic

Messier-Dowty Ltd v Sabena SA [2000] 1 WLR 2040

notes: Agency worker employment status split decision; implied contract with end-user left open though Council claim not appealed.

enrichment.short_title: Agency cleaner's employment status for unfair dismissal
key_facts: Mrs Dacas worked exclusively as a cleaner at a Wandsworth mental health hostel for about four years through Brook Street Bureau.
She was paid by Brook Street under a Temporary Worker Agreement expressed to be a contract for services, while Wandsworth exercised day-to-day control.
Wandsworth requested her withdrawal after a conduct complaint and Brook Street ceased finding her work.
The employment tribunal held she was neither Brook Street's nor the council's employee; the EAT held she was employed by Brook Street.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by the employment agency against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision remitting an unfair dismissal claim.
enrichment.outcome: Brook Street's appeal allowed; Mrs Dacas was not an employee of Brook Street, but her unappealed tribunal dismissal against Wandsworth stands despite the court indicating an implied contract with the end-user may exist in similar cases.
enrichment.ratio: In triangular agency arrangements an express contract for services with the agency is not necessarily a contract of employment; tribunals must consider whether an implied contract of service exists with the end-user where the worker works exclusively under its control, but mutuality requiring the end-user to remunerate the worker may prevent such implication under established authority.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Dacas worked under a contract of service with Brook Street
Whether an implied contract of employment existed with Wandsworth Borough Council
Application of Ready Mixed Concrete, Carmichael and Montgomery v Johnson Underwood
Whether control and payment split between agency and end-user precludes employment status

notes: Race discrimination appeal dismissed; Hendricks continuing-act test correctly applied on full merits hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Race discrimination appeal: time limits and continuing acts
key_facts: Keith Henry, a part-time library assistant at London Borough of Newham, alleged racial discrimination over several years.
Complaints included time-keeping monitoring, handling of a complaint against a manager, OHS attendance, use of biblical quotations, and disciplinary proceedings.
The employment tribunal rejected institutional racism and found specific incidents were either out of time or not discriminatory.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissed his appeal; he appealed on Hendricks continuing-act and monitoring findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissing a race discrimination claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal correctly applied section 68(7)(b) on a full merits hearing and its findings of fact on monitoring and other incidents were not vitiated by legal error.
enrichment.ratio: On a full merits hearing, a tribunal may properly conclude that linked but causally connected incidents do not amount to an act extending over a period under section 68(7)(b) where each incident is found not to involve racial discrimination; Hendricks does not require treating discrete allegations as a continuing act absent evidence of an ongoing discriminatory state of affairs.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal misapplied the continuing act test in section 68(7)(b)
Whether Hendricks required cumulative consideration of out-of-time allegations
Whether monitoring findings of fact were perverse
Whether Mr Burbage's handling of whistleblowing letters was discriminatory
linked_authorities: Hendricks v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis [2003] IRLR 96
Anya v University of Oxford [2001] IRLR 377

confidence.notes: Appeal grounds and tribunal findings are clearly summarised, though many factual complaints were not pursued on appeal.
